summary:
Public Law 118-157, the Improving Federal Building Security Act of 2024, establishes a procedural framework compelling Facility Security Committees (FSCs) to formally respond to security recommendations issued by the Federal Protective Service (FPS) and imposes related reporting and monitoring obligations on the Secretary of Homeland Security. The Act is a freestanding measure, designated as a note to 40 U.S.C. 1315, and does not codify amendments to the United States Code.

Section 2(a) defines “Facility Security Committee” as a committee composed of representatives of all federal tenants in a specific non-military facility, the facility security organization, and the owning or leasing federal tenant, responsible for addressing facility-specific security issues and approving security measures. “Agency” adopts the definition in 5 U.S.C. § 551, and “Secretary” means the Secretary of Homeland Security.

Section 2(b) imposes a duty on the head of an FSC, or a designee, to respond to the Secretary not later than 90 days after FPS issues a facility security recommendation. The response must indicate whether the FSC intends to adopt or reject the recommendation and describe the financial implications, including whether the benefits outweigh the costs. If rejection is intended, the FSC must provide a justification for accepting the resulting risk. The Secretary is required to develop a monitoring method for these recommendations and responses and to take reasonable action to ensure FSC responsiveness.

Section 2(c) requires the Secretary to submit an annual report to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and the House Committees on Homeland Security and Transportation and Infrastructure. The first report is due not later than 270 days after enactment, and annually thereafter, covering the preceding fiscal year. The report must contain: a summary of FPS security recommendations; the percentages accepted and rejected; the percentage of FSCs failing to respond timely; a summary of rejection justifications; a summary of financial implications of responses; an analysis of mitigation steps taken for rejected recommendations; and an analysis of trends. Reports are to be unclassified but may include a classified annex. An annual briefing to the same committees is also mandated.

Section 2(d) requires a one-time unredacted report within 180 days of enactment on all surveillance technology recommended by FPS and its intended use.

Section 2(e) provides that no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out the Act. Section 2(f) contains a sunset provision: the Act ceases to be effective five years after enactment, and the Comptroller General must submit a report to Congress on the Act’s effectiveness not later than that date. Section 2(g) limits applicability to General Services Administration facilities under FPS protection and non-GSA facilities that pay fees to FPS for protection.
